headquarters: New York, United States (European HQ in London, United Kingdom)
sector: AI / Voice AI / Audio Generation / Creative Technology / Enterprise SaaS
ai_use_case: ElevenLabs is a voice AI and audio generation platform that solves the problem of producing natural, human-quality speech and audio content at scale. The platform addresses multiple use cases: (1) Text-to-Speech (TTS) — the core offering, generating lifelike speech with nuanced intonation, emotional awareness, and natural pauses in 70+ languages. Used by publishers (HarperCollins), media companies (Washington Post, TIME), and content creators for audiobooks, podcasts, and video narration. (2) AI Dubbing — automated video/audio translation into 29 languages while preserving the original speaker's voice, emotions, and intonation, enabling content creators and studios to reach global audiences without hiring multilingual voiceover talent. (3) Conversational AI — a developer platform for building and deploying interactive voice agents that handle inbound and outbound calls with ultra-low latency (~75ms for flash model), used by enterprises like Deutsche Telekom and Revolut for customer service automation. The platform handles 50,000+ calls per month across deployed enterprise environments. (4) Voice Cloning — enables users to create custom voice profiles from audio samples, with applications in content personalization, brand voice consistency, and accessibility. (5) AI Music and Sound Effects — Eleven Music generates studio-grade music from text prompts, and AI Sound Effects creates ambience and audio cues from text descriptions. (6) Studio 3.0 — a unified browser-based editor combining voiceovers, music, sound effects, captioning, and video editing into a single collaborative workflow. The company has evolved from a text-to-speech tool into a comprehensive audio AI platform serving the entire audio content creation pipeline.
ai_technology_used: Proprietary deep learning models built in-house by a specialized research team. Key models and technologies include: (1) Eleven v3 (June 2025) — the latest and most advanced TTS model, built from the ground up with diffusion-based architecture supporting 70+ languages, natural multi-speaker dialogue, emotional range (sighing, whispering, laughing), and audio tags for fine-grained control. (2) Earlier models (Eleven v1, v2, Turbo v2.5, Flash v2.5) optimized for different tradeoffs between quality and latency. Flash v2.5 achieves ~75ms time-to-first-audio for real-time conversational use cases. (3) Proprietary speaker diarization models for detecting and separating multiple speakers in audio. (4) Background noise removal and music/dialogue separation models. (5) Speech-to-text systems trained on proprietary labeled data. (6) AI Speech Classifier for detecting AI-generated audio. (7) Content moderation AI classifiers for safety monitoring. The company invested heavily in proprietary data pipelines, working with voice coaches to label emotional content, building what they consider a more defensible moat than model architecture alone. The research team has published work at venues like NeurIPS. Infrastructure supports real-time inference with sub-second latency across global deployments.
build_vs_buy: Fully built in-house. All core AI models (TTS, dubbing, voice cloning, conversational AI, music generation, sound effects, speech classifier, content moderation) are developed internally by a dedicated research team. Co-founder Piotr Dabkowski (ex-Google ML engineer, Oxford/Cambridge educated, NeurIPS 2017 author) leads research, maintaining an elite team of AI researchers focused exclusively on audio AI. The company builds the full vertical stack: proprietary generative models, voice rendering pipeline, web-based platform, API infrastructure, enterprise deployment tools, and trust/safety systems. The only external components integrated are cloud infrastructure for hosting, third-party LLMs hosted within their Conversational AI agent platform (for the language understanding component of voice agents), and CRM/telephony integrations (Salesforce, Stripe, Zendesk, Twilio). ElevenLabs also selectively collaborates with academia (UC Berkeley) on open-source safety tooling and detection models.
implementation_timeline: April 2022: Co-founded by Mati Staniszewski (ex-Palantir) and Piotr Dabkowski (ex-Google) in New York, both childhood friends from Warsaw, Poland. Motivated by the poor quality of dubbed American films they watched growing up. Spent 2022 developing initial audio AI models. January 2023: Launched beta platform; attracted over 1 million users within 5 months. January 2023: $2M pre-seed round. June 2023: $19M Series A led by Nat Friedman, Daniel Gross, and Andreessen Horowitz, with new products including Projects (long-form content tool) and Voice Library marketplace. August 2023: Expanded to 28 languages. October 2023: Launched AI Dubbing in 20+ languages. January 2024: $80M Series B at $1.1B valuation (unicorn status achieved). June 2024: Launched ElevenLabs Reader App (iOS/Android). July 2024: Released Voice Isolator. November 2024: Released Conversational AI platform for voice agents. January 2025: $180M Series C at $3.3B valuation. February 2025: Launched AI-generated audiobook creation platform. June 2025: Released Eleven v3 (70+ languages, audio tags). August 2025: Launched Eleven Music. September 2025: Released Studio 3.0 unified audio/video editor. September 2025: Employee tender offer at $6.6B valuation. November 2025: Announced partnerships with iconic Hollywood actors for voice marketplace. February 2026: $500M Series D at $11B valuation, led by Sequoia Capital. Total funding: $781M across 5 rounds. IPO targeted for 2027-2028.
integration_approach: Platform play with multi-modal delivery. ElevenLabs operates as a self-service web platform with tiered SaaS subscriptions, a comprehensive developer API, and enterprise custom deployments. Integration options include: (1) Web Platform — browser-based Studio 3.0 editor for end-to-end audio/video content creation; (2) REST API — full programmatic access to TTS, dubbing, voice cloning, conversational AI, sound effects, and music generation, enabling developers to embed voice capabilities into any application; (3) SDKs and libraries in Python, JavaScript, and other languages; (4) Conversational AI Agent Platform — connects to CRM (Salesforce), support desks (Zendesk), calendars, payment systems (Stripe), and telephony providers (Twilio) via pre-built integrations; (5) Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration for AI agent ecosystems; (6) ElevenLabs Reader App — standalone consumer product for text-to-audio conversion; (7) Voice Library Marketplace — a two-sided marketplace where voice creators license their voices and developers/creators purchase them; (8) Enterprise deployments with dedicated engineering support, forward-deployed teams, regional data residency (US, EU, India), and private environments. Pricing ranges from free tier (10,000 characters/month) to enterprise custom contracts reaching $2M+.
quantified_roi: ElevenLabs crossed $330M annual recurring revenue (ARR) by end of 2025, up from approximately $120M at end of 2024 — representing ~175% year-over-year growth. The company took only 5 months to go from $200M to $330M ARR. Enterprise revenue grew 200% year-over-year. Valuation trajectory: $1.1B (January 2024) to $3.3B (January 2025) to $6.6B (September 2025 tender) to $11B (February 2026) — a 10x increase in just 2 years. Total funding raised: $781M across 5 rounds (pre-seed through Series D). The company serves 75%+ of Fortune 500 companies (up from 41% in 2024). Largest enterprise contracts have reached $2M. Users have generated over 1,000 years of audio content on the platform in just two years. Revenue per employee is exceptionally high: ~$330M ARR with ~690 employees yields ~$478K ARR per employee. The platform targets a $660M+ ARR run rate for 2026 (projected doubling). The company's 0-to-$330M ARR in approximately 3 years is one of the fastest revenue ramp-ups in SaaS history, comparable to the growth trajectories of companies like Figma and Notion.
before_after_comparison: Before ElevenLabs: Traditional voiceover and dubbing required hiring professional voice actors, booking recording studios, and managing post-production editing. A single audiobook narration could cost $5,000-$15,000 and take weeks. Dubbing a film or video series into 10 languages required 10 separate voiceover sessions with native-speaking actors, multiplying costs and timelines linearly. Enterprise customer service relied on human agents or rigid IVR systems with robotic-sounding prompts. Content creators had to choose between expensive professional voice talent or low-quality robotic TTS. Multilingual content was a luxury reserved for large media companies with significant budgets. After ElevenLabs: A content creator types text into a browser and receives natural, emotionally expressive audio in seconds. An audiobook can be narrated in minutes rather than weeks. A single video can be dubbed into 29 languages simultaneously while preserving the original speaker's voice, emotions, and timing. Enterprise voice agents handle 50,000+ calls per month with natural-sounding AI voices that understand context and emotion. Independent YouTube creators build successful channels using only AI-generated narration. Publishing houses like HarperCollins produce audiobooks at a fraction of previous cost. The shift from per-project physical production to software-based generation transforms audio content from a capital-intensive project into an operational workflow accessible to anyone.
scale_of_deployment: ElevenLabs serves millions of individual users and thousands of businesses. Enterprise adoption spans 75%+ of Fortune 500 companies (as of early 2026), including named clients such as Deutsche Telekom, Revolut, Washington Post, TIME, HarperCollins, Paradox Interactive (gaming), and Bertelsmann. The platform supports 70+ languages and over 5,000 AI voices. Users have generated over 1,000 years (8.7+ million hours) of audio content in two years of operation. Conversational AI deployments handle 50,000+ calls per month across enterprise environments. The company employs approximately 690 people (as of January 2026) across 14+ global offices: New York (US HQ), London (European HQ), San Francisco, Warsaw, Dublin, Tokyo, Seoul, Singapore, Bengaluru, Sydney, Sao Paulo, Berlin, Paris, and Mexico City. The ElevenLabs Reader App extends reach to mobile consumers on iOS and Android. The Voice Library marketplace creates a two-sided ecosystem connecting voice creators with content producers at scale.
revenue_model_change: ElevenLabs has undergone three fundamental revenue model expansions: (1) From TTS tool to audio platform — originally a text-to-speech product, ElevenLabs expanded into dubbing, voice cloning, conversational AI, music generation, and sound effects, creating multiple monetization vectors from a single platform. Revenue streams now include subscription SaaS (tiered plans from free to enterprise), API usage-based pricing (per character processed or per call minute), Voice Library marketplace commissions (shared revenue with voice creators and licensed celebrity voices), enterprise custom contracts (up to $2M+), and Reader App subscriptions. (2) From prosumer to enterprise — while maintaining a freemium self-serve motion that drives individual adoption, the company's growth engine shifted decisively toward enterprise contracts. Enterprise revenue grew 200% YoY, with Fortune 500 penetration rising from 41% to 75%+. Enterprise clients pay for dedicated support, regional data residency, custom voice development, and volume commitments. (3) From generation tool to voice agent platform — the November 2024 launch of Conversational AI opened an entirely new revenue stream in the enterprise voice automation market (call centers, customer service, sales), which represents a significantly larger addressable market than content creation. This pivot from content generation to real-time agent infrastructure positions ElevenLabs to capture recurring enterprise automation spend rather than one-time content production budgets.
key_success_factor: The single most important factor in ElevenLabs' success was the research-first approach that delivered genuinely superior voice quality, combined with aggressive platform expansion that turned a single capability (TTS) into an indispensable audio infrastructure layer. Unlike competitors who treated voice as a feature of a larger platform, ElevenLabs built a dedicated team of elite audio AI researchers who focused exclusively on voice quality — replicating human elements like natural pauses, laughter, conversational fillers, emotional variation, and breaths that competitors could not match. This quality advantage was validated by independent benchmarks: a 75.3% listener preference rate on HuggingFace TTS Arena across nearly 20,000 blind test votes. But quality alone would not have created an $11B company. The critical strategic move was rapidly expanding from TTS into dubbing (October 2023), conversational AI (November 2024), and music/sound effects (2025), creating a platform that enterprises adopt for multiple use cases rather than a point solution they can easily switch. The resulting data flywheel — millions of hours of generated speech improving models, and a growing Voice Library marketplace creating network effects — built compounding competitive advantages that get stronger with each new user.
main_challenge: The dual challenge of safety/misuse management and competitive commoditization. ElevenLabs' core technology — the ability to clone and generate hyper-realistic human voices — is inherently dual-use. Early misuse incidents included deepfake audio clips mimicking celebrities (Emma Watson, Joe Rogan) used for harassment and misinformation, and a cloned voice successfully fooling a bank's voice authentication system. The Vacker v. ElevenLabs lawsuit (the first AI copyright case to reach settlement) alleged unauthorized use of audiobook narrators' voices to train AI models, highlighting IP and consent risks. The company's Terms of Service controversy in early 2025 — where language granting 'perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free' license to user voice recordings sparked backlash — demonstrates the ongoing tension between platform growth and user trust. On the competitive front, while ElevenLabs maintains a quality lead, the TTS space is increasingly crowded: OpenAI, Google, Amazon Polly, Microsoft Azure, Cartesia, LMNT, Murf, Play.ht, and open-source alternatives (StyleTTS2, Tortoise-TTS) are all improving rapidly. Amazon Polly delivers 85% of ElevenLabs' quality at 1/10th the cost. The risk of voice AI commoditization is real, making the platform expansion beyond TTS (into agents, music, studio tools) a strategic necessity rather than a luxury.
ethical_or_regulatory_issue: ElevenLabs faces significant ethical and regulatory challenges across multiple dimensions: (1) Deepfake and misinformation risk — the technology enables creation of convincing fake audio of real people, with documented cases of celebrity voice cloning for harassment and a cloned voice fooling bank authentication. (2) Voice actor rights and copyright — the Vacker v. ElevenLabs lawsuit (filed 2024, settled 2025) was the first of 48 AI copyright lawsuits to reach settlement, involving two audiobook narrators whose voices were allegedly used without consent to create 'Adam' and 'Bella' default voices, setting a legal precedent for AI voice IP. (3) Terms of Service controversy — the 2025 ToS backlash over 'perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free' licensing of user voice recordings highlighted consent and data ownership concerns. (4) EU AI Act compliance — voice cloning and synthetic speech generation trigger transparency obligations under Article 50 (AI-generated audio must be marked in machine-readable format and disclosed to end users). ElevenLabs acknowledges EU AI Act applicability in its prohibited use policy and offers EU data residency. (5) GDPR implications — biometric voice data processing requires clear legal bases and consent frameworks. (6) Safety countermeasures — ElevenLabs maintains a 'No-Go Voices' list blocking cloning of high-risk voices (celebrities, politicians), requires technological verification for Professional Voice Cloning, monitors via AI classifiers and human reviewers, built an AI Speech Classifier detection tool, and collaborated with UC Berkeley on safety research. Despite these measures, the fundamental tension between making voice AI accessible and preventing misuse remains unresolved.
lesson_for_entrepreneurs: Build proprietary data pipelines and quality labeling methodology as your moat — model architectures commoditize, but curated data and platform network effects compound over time.

one_slide_summary: Founded in 2022 by two Polish childhood friends frustrated by poorly dubbed American films, ElevenLabs built AI voices so realistic they achieved a 75% preference rate over all competitors in blind listening tests. From a TTS tool to a full audio AI platform (dubbing, voice agents, music, sound effects), the company reached $330M ARR in just 3 years and an $11B valuation — but the same technology that powers HarperCollins audiobooks and Deutsche Telekom voice agents has also been used for celebrity deepfakes and sparked the first-ever AI voice copyright settlement, making ElevenLabs a textbook case of dual-use AI technology where commercial success and ethical risk are inseparable.
competitive_moat: Four-layer moat: (1) Voice quality leadership — independently validated #1 position on HuggingFace TTS Arena with 75.3% listener preference across 20,000 blind votes, maintained by a specialized research team focused exclusively on audio AI; (2) Proprietary data flywheel — millions of hours of generated speech, user feedback, and curated emotional labeling data improve models continuously, creating a self-reinforcing quality advantage that new entrants cannot replicate; (3) Platform breadth and switching costs — expansion from TTS into dubbing, voice cloning, conversational AI, music, sound effects, and Studio 3.0 creates deep enterprise integration across multiple workflows, making replacement increasingly costly; (4) Voice Library marketplace network effects — a two-sided marketplace connecting voice creators (including licensed Hollywood actors) with businesses and developers, where more voice options attract more users, generating more compensation for providers, creating a virtuous cycle. The combination of research excellence, data advantages, platform lock-in, and marketplace dynamics creates compound moats that neither big-tech competitors (who treat voice as a secondary feature) nor startups (who lack the data and distribution) can easily match.
open_vs_proprietary_strategy: Primarily proprietary with selective open collaboration. All core AI models (TTS, dubbing, voice cloning, conversational AI, music generation, content moderation) are closed-source and available only through the ElevenLabs platform and API. This is a deliberate strategic choice driven by: (1) Safety — open-sourcing hyper-realistic voice generation models would enable unconstrained deepfake creation without any moderation safeguards; (2) Competitive protection — the voice models and proprietary data pipelines are ElevenLabs' core IP; (3) Quality control — maintaining a closed platform allows consistent quality guarantees and enterprise SLAs. However, ElevenLabs engages in selective openness: the API is extensively documented and developer-friendly, they host open-source LLMs within their Conversational AI platform alongside proprietary TTS/STT models, they collaborated with UC Berkeley on AI safety detection tools, and they published the AI Speech Classifier. The company also supports the Model Context Protocol (MCP) standard for agent interoperability. This 'proprietary core, open ecosystem' approach maximizes monetization of the voice AI technology while building an open developer platform around it.
data_strategy: ElevenLabs' data strategy operates across four tiers: (1) Licensed professional recordings — the foundation of model training, using commercially licensed voice recordings with explicit consent. Voice actors for the Voice Library marketplace license their voices and receive revenue share per usage. High-profile partnerships with Hollywood actors for the Iconic Voice marketplace involve rights holders approving scripts and uses before audio is generated. (2) Proprietary labeled data — ElevenLabs invested heavily in building custom data pipelines, working with voice coaches to label emotional content, tone, pacing, and conversational nuances. This labeling methodology is considered more defensible than model architecture. (3) User-generated data — voices uploaded by users for cloning, though the company's Terms of Service controversially included broad licensing language. Professional Voice Cloning requires technological verification to prevent unauthorized use of others' voices. (4) Platform usage data — the millions of hours of generated audio and user feedback create a continuous improvement loop for model quality. The Vacker v. ElevenLabs settlement highlighted the risks of training data sourcing, particularly regarding audiobook recordings processed without narrator consent. The company now maintains stricter consent frameworks, 'No-Go Voices' blocklists, and GDPR-compliant data residency options (US, EU, India) for enterprise clients.
eu_ai_act_risk_category: Limited-risk AI with GPAI (General Purpose AI) model obligations. ElevenLabs' voice generation and cloning technology triggers transparency requirements under Article 50 of the EU AI Act: (1) Provider obligation — AI systems generating synthetic audio must ensure outputs are marked in machine-readable format as artificially generated or manipulated; (2) Deployer obligation — users creating synthetic voice content must disclose to end users that the audio is AI-generated; (3) GPAI model obligations — as a provider of general-purpose AI models (used across diverse applications from audiobooks to customer service agents), ElevenLabs must maintain technical documentation and provide a public summary of training content, while complying with EU copyright rules. Voice cloning specifically has been classified by EU guidance as a high-attention application requiring transparency measures and consent frameworks. ElevenLabs proactively addresses compliance through its Prohibited Use Policy (explicitly referencing EU AI Act Regulation 2024/1689), No-Go Voices system, AI Speech Classifier for detection, and EU data residency. The company is not classified as prohibited or high-risk under its intended use, but individual deployments (e.g., impersonation, biometric identification) could trigger higher risk categories. Full EU AI Act enforcement begins August 2, 2026.
workforce_impact: ElevenLabs itself is a significant job creator, growing to approximately 690 employees by January 2026 across 14+ offices globally, with 50+ open positions. The company plans further expansion with locally embedded go-to-market teams in each city. However, the broader workforce impact is disruptive: (1) Voice acting displacement — the voiceover industry faces existential pressure as AI can now produce broadcast-quality narration at a fraction of the cost. Publishing houses like HarperCollins using ElevenLabs for audiobooks directly reduces demand for human narrators. The Vacker lawsuit illustrated voice actors' fears of being replaced by AI trained on their own performances. (2) Dubbing industry transformation — AI dubbing into 29 languages threatens the livelihoods of thousands of professional dubbing actors globally. (3) Call center automation — Conversational AI handling 50,000+ calls per month across enterprise deployments replaces human call center agents. (4) New roles created — the platform democratizes audio content creation, enabling marketers, educators, and content creators who previously could not afford professional voiceover to produce audio content. The Voice Library marketplace creates a new (if potentially less lucrative) compensation model for voice professionals who license their voices. Overall, ElevenLabs exemplifies the 'creative AI displacement' pattern where technology simultaneously destroys traditional roles while enabling entirely new categories of creators.
energy_and_sustainability_impact: No company-specific sustainability data has been published by ElevenLabs. As an AI inference-heavy platform generating millions of hours of audio content, ElevenLabs' environmental footprint primarily comes from GPU compute for model inference across its global infrastructure. Audio generation models generally require less compute than image or video generation models, suggesting a relatively lower per-request energy footprint compared to AI video platforms. However, the sheer volume of generation (1,000+ years of audio in 2 years, 50,000+ voice agent calls per month) creates meaningful aggregate energy consumption. The shift from physical recording studios (with travel, lighting, equipment) to software-based generation likely reduces the per-unit carbon footprint of audio content production, similar to Synthesia's claims for video. The company runs on cloud infrastructure (specific provider not disclosed) across multiple global regions. [uncertain]
